issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: Compulsive exercise is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other selected items cluster around hypervigilance, dissociation, memory disorganisation, and danger-based appraisals after terrorism. Excessive exercise does not clearly serve or connect to those symptoms, making it look like a strategy for a different presentation unless additional context were present.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is disproportionately severe relative to the rest of the selected profile and is not well supported by the surrounding appraisals. The other appraisals focus on danger and bodily unreliability, while the threat/memory items emphasize hyperarousal and fragmented recall. This suicidal-hopelessness appraisal can occur in PTSD, but here it stands out as insufficiently linked to the rest of the formulation and item set.

vignette:
Valeria was twenty-one when the bomb went off in the food court. She had been on her lunch break, standing in line at the taco stand, when the pressure wave threw her against a concrete pillar. She remembers the sound—not as an explosion, but as a physical force that erased everything else—and then the dust, so thick she could taste metal. What she cannot remember, no matter how hard she tries, is the next several minutes. She knows from news reports that people were running, that first responders arrived, that she was found sitting on the floor with her hands over her ears. But that part of her own life is a blank, a torn-out page. When she tries to describe what happened to anyone, the words simply will not come; she knows the facts, can see the images in her mind, but her throat closes and her mouth goes dry as though the event itself has stolen her language.

In the weeks afterward, Valeria returned to her job at the warehouse. She had always been a quiet, focused worker, but now her focus took on a different quality. She began to notice things she had never noticed before: the way a coworker would lift a box too quickly, the sudden pivot of a forklift, the sharp clang of metal shelving being loaded. Each sudden movement sent a jolt through her chest, a spike of alarm that left her hands trembling. She started scanning the warehouse floor constantly, her eyes moving from one corner to the next, checking for anything out of place—a pallet left in an aisle, a loose strap, a person approaching from behind. She had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, that danger could arrive without warning, and that the only way to survive was to be ready at all times. This vigilance exhausted her, but she could not stop.

She also found herself avoiding eye contact. At first it was subtle—she would look at her supervisor’s shoulder instead of his face, at the label on a box instead of a coworker’s eyes. But over time it became automatic. Looking someone in the eyes felt like exposure, like letting them see that she was fragile, that she was waiting for something terrible to happen. She was certain that if people saw her fear, they would use it against her, or worse, that they would confirm what she already suspected: that she could no longer trust herself. Her own body had betrayed her during the attack—it had frozen, it had failed to run, it had sat uselessly on a dirty floor while others fled. She now believed that her body was unreliable, that she could not count on it to protect her, and that she had to monitor it constantly for signs of weakness.

At night, the vigilance sharpened. Valeria found it harder to feel safe after dark. She checked the locks on her apartment door three times before bed. She kept a light on in the hallway. She lay awake listening to the building’s sounds—the groan of pipes, the footsteps of a neighbor—each noise a potential threat. Sometimes, when the anxiety became unbearable, she deliberately tried to leave her own body, to blank out, to float away from the fear. It was the only way she knew to escape when there was nowhere to run. But the dissociation left her feeling hollow and disconnected, as though she were watching her own life from a great distance.

When she did remember the event—and she could not always control when it came—what surfaced most was not fear but rage. A hot, wordless fury at the people who had done this, at the randomness of it, at the fact that her life had been split into before and after. The rage frightened her because it felt as uncontrollable as the explosion itself. She had no outlet for it, no way to speak it, because she could not find the words.

What finally brought Valeria to seek help was not the anger or the scanning or the sleepless nights. It was the eye contact. A supervisor had pulled her aside and asked why she would not look at anyone. He said it seemed like she was hiding something, or that she did not care. Valeria realized that her survival strategy—her constant scanning, her refusal to meet eyes—was being read as hostility or indifference. She was afraid of losing her job. But more than that, she was afraid that she was becoming someone she did not recognize: a person who could not trust, could not speak, could not rest. She wanted to feel safe again, or at least to stop feeling like a target every moment of every day. She was not sure if that was possible. But she was willing to try.
